body.stem: You have a resource group named RG-Production. A team member needs to spin up and manage IaaS compute resources and their disks in this resource group. The team member must not be able to modify networks or storage accounts connected to these resources, and must not be able to grant access to other users. Which built-in role should you assign at the resource group scope?

exhibit.text:
PS C:\> Get-AzRoleAssignment -ResourceGroupName 'RG-Production' |
      Select-Object SignInName,RoleDefinitionName,Scope |
      Format-Table -AutoSize

SignInName              Definition                              Scope
---------               ----------                              -----
alice@contoso.com       Owner                                   /subscriptions/00000000-.../RG-Production
bob@contoso.com         Reader                                  /subscriptions/00000000-.../RG-Production

explanation.correct: Virtual Machine Contributor grants the ability to create and manage VMs and their disks, including resetting the root password and managing local user accounts using VM extensions, but it does not grant access to the connected virtual network or storage account and does not allow assigning roles in Azure RBAC. This satisfies the requirement to manage compute resources without access to networks or storage, and without the ability to grant access to other users.

perChoice.a: Owner grants full access to all resources, including the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC, which violates the requirement that the team member must not be able to grant access to other users.
perChoice.b: Contributor grants full access to manage all resources, including networks and storage accounts, which violates the requirement that the team member must not modify the networks or storage accounts connected to the resources.
perChoice.d: Reader is read-only and does not allow the team member to create or manage any compute resources at all.

body.stem: A security operations team must be able to grant users and groups privileges to Azure resources by assigning built-in definitions at any scope in your tenant, including subscriptions added in the future. The team must not be able to create or modify Azure resources themselves, and must only manage access through Azure RBAC (not via other paths such as Azure Policy). Which built-in definition and scope should you assign?

exhibit.text:
Scopes in your tenant:
  /
  /subscriptions/Sub-Production
  /subscriptions/Sub-Production/resourceGroups/RG-Identity
  /subscriptions/Sub-Production/resourceGroups/RG-Web

Planned scope for the operations team: entire tenant (including all current and future subscriptions)

options.text: User Access Administrator at the root scope (/)
Role Based Access Control Administrator at the root scope (/)

explanation.correct: Role Based Access Control Administrator manages access to Azure resources by assigning roles using Azure RBAC, and is scoped at the root so it applies to all current and future subscriptions. It is restricted to RBAC only and does not allow managing access via other mechanisms such as Azure Policy, and it does not permit creating or modifying Azure resources.

perChoice.a: Owner grants full access to all resources plus the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC. This violates the requirement that the team must not create or modify Azure resources.
perChoice.b: User Access Administrator lets you manage user access to Azure resources, but it is broader than RBAC and can include other access management paths, whereas the requirement is to only manage access through Azure RBAC.
perChoice.d: Contributor grants full access to manage all resources but does not allow assigning roles in Azure RBAC, so the team could not grant users access.

body.stem: A company wants to grant an external contractor view-only access to blob data in a specific storage account, using Microsoft Entra authentication. The contractor needs to view containers and list blobs. The contractor must NOT be able to write, delete, or modify any blobs. Which built-in role should be assigned at the storage account scope?

explanation.correct: Storage Blob Data Reader grants read and list access to Azure Storage containers and blobs. It is a data-plane role used through Microsoft Entra authentication and does not allow writing, deleting, or modifying any blob data, which matches the view-only contractor requirement.

perChoice.a: Storage Blob Data Contributor allows read, write, and delete on containers and blobs. This violates the requirement that the contractor must not write, delete, or modify blobs.
perChoice.c: Storage Blob Data Owner provides full access to blob containers and data including assigning POSIX access control. This grants write and delete permissions and goes well beyond view-only access.
perChoice.d: Storage Account Contributor permits management of the storage account itself and provides access to the account key, which can be used to access data via Shared Key authorization rather than through Microsoft Entra authentication.

body.stem: A cloud operations team needs to handle daily backup operations - creating and managing backups, restoring data when requested. The team also needs to be able to remove backed up data when retention policies require it. The team must NOT be able to create new backup vaults or grant access to other users. Which built-in role should be assigned?

exhibit.text:
Environment summary
-------------------
Recovery Services vault:     prod-backup-vault
Location:                    eastus
Identity used by team:       ops-backup-group

Protected items in vault:
  - vm-app01        (Daily, 7-day retention)
  - vm-app02        (Daily, 14-day retention)
  - fileshare-team  (Hourly, 30-day retention)

explanation.correct: Backup Contributor lets you manage the backup service, including creating, restoring, and removing backed up data, but cannot create vaults or grant access to other users. This matches the requirement for the team to perform daily backup operations and also remove backed up data on demand.

perChoice.b: Backup Operator lets you manage backup services except for the removal of backup data, in addition to the same restrictions on vault creation and granting access. It cannot remove backed up data, so it does not satisfy the retention-removal requirement.
perChoice.c: Backup Reader can only view backup services and cannot make changes, so it does not allow the team to perform any backup or restore actions.
perChoice.d: Owner grants full access to all resources and the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC, including the ability to create vaults and give access to others, which violates two of the stated restrictions.

body.stem: A user, alice@contoso.com, has the Contributor definition assigned at the subscription scope and the Reader definition assigned at a specific resource group within that subscription. According to how Azure's access system handles privileges across overlapping scopes, what is the user's effective privilege within the resource group?

exhibit.text:
$ az role assignment list --assignee alice@contoso.com -o table
Principal              Definition     Scope
---------              ----------     -----
alice@contoso.com      Contributor    /subscriptions/Sub-Production
alice@contoso.com      Reader         /subscriptions/Sub-Production/resourceGroups/RG-Web

options.text: Only Contributor actions, because the subscription-scope definition supersedes resource group-scope definitions.
Only Reader actions, because the more specific resource group scope overrides the higher-scope definition.
The combined actions of both definitions under the additive Azure RBAC model.
No actions, because two definitions at different scopes are in conflict and cancel each other out.

explanation.correct: Azure RBAC is an additive model, so the user's effective privileges are the sum of the role assignments that apply. Both the subscription-scope Contributor definition and the resource group-scope Reader definition apply, so the user has the combined actions available to them inside the resource group.

perChoice.a: Subscriptions-scoped assignments do not supersede more specific scopes, and Azure RBAC does not work by having a higher scope override lower scopes.
perChoice.b: A more specific scope does not replace or override a higher-scope definition in Azure RBAC. Both assignments apply additively.
perChoice.d: Azure RBAC does not cancel assignments when scopes overlap; overlapping assignments are combined, not subtracted.

body.stem: You have a landing-zone team that owns the virtual networks in the resource group rg-platform. As demand changes they must reconfigure addressing and adjust the security rules of those networks, but virtual machines are delivered by a separate operations team and handing out permissions belongs to the security team. This tenant has been fully migrated to Azure Resource Manager, so no legacy networking resources exist. Which built-in role should you assign to the landing-zone team at the scope of rg-platform?

columns: Operation the landing-zone team needs to perform
rows: Create a virtual network and add subnets to it
Change the network security rules applied to a subnet
Attach a network interface to an existing subnet
Deploy a virtual machine into one of those subnets
Create a role assignment for a colleague

explanation.correct: Network Contributor lets a principal manage networks but not access to them, and the built-in role explicitly does not grant permission to deploy or manage virtual machines, so the team can create the virtual network, add subnets, adjust network security rules and attach network interfaces while being stopped from deploying VMs. It also contains no permission to grant access to others.

perChoice.b: Virtual Machine Contributor creates and manages virtual machines, disks and VM extensions, but it explicitly does not grant management access to the virtual network or storage account the virtual machines connect to, so the landing-zone team would not be able to create subnets or change network security rules.
perChoice.c: Classic Network Contributor only covers classic (legacy) networks, and this scenario is entirely built on current resource-manager virtual networks, subnets and network interfaces.
perChoice.d: Contributor grants full access to manage all resources, which would let the team deploy virtual machines as well, contradicting the requirement. It only withholds the right to assign roles.

body.stem: You have a deployment pipeline that runs on a Microsoft-hosted agent under the managed identity svc-fabrikam-deploy, as shown in the excerpt. It must be able to enumerate repositories, read their tags, and download images from the registry fabrikamregistry. The security team requires that this identity never uploads new images and never removes existing repositories, tags, or manifests. Which built-in role should you assign to the identity at the scope of that registry?

exhibit.text:
# fabrikam-api / azure-pipelines.yml  (excerpt)
steps:
  - task: AzureCLI@2
    displayName: Prepare agent
    inputs:
      azureSubscription: 'svc-fabrikam-deploy'
      scriptType: bash
      inlineScript: |
        REG=fabrikamregistry
        az acr repository list --name $REG --output table
        az acr repository show-tags --name $REG --repository api --output table
        docker pull $REG.azurecr.io/api:2.9.0
        docker pull $REG.azurecr.io/api:2.9.1

explanation.correct: AcrPull is the built-in definition for pulling artifacts from a container registry. It lets the pipeline enumerate repositories, read tags and download images, and it carries no write permissions on the registry content, so the identity cannot upload images or delete repositories, tags or manifests, which is what the security team requires.

perChoice.b: AcrPush grants the ability to push artifacts to a registry (as well as pulling them). Uploading images is precisely what the security team prohibits, so this definition is too broad.
perChoice.c: AcrQuarantineReader only pulls quarantined images. The pipeline needs the ordinary, non-quarantined images in fabrikamregistry, so this role doesn't meet the functional requirement.
perChoice.d: AcrQuarantineWriter pushes artifacts to a registry (quarantined ones) and pulls quarantined images. It permits uploading, which violates the security requirement, and it doesn't cover the normal images the pipeline uses.

body.stem: You have a storage platform team that works from a runbook in the resource group rg-storage-prod. They stand up accounts, tighten their firewall configuration, change access tiers, and switch on diagnostic settings as part of normal operations. Company policy states that this team must never receive the permissions that reach container or blob content through Microsoft Entra authentication. Which built-in role should you assign to the team at the scope of rg-storage-prod?

columns: Activity in the storage platform runbook
rows: Create a storage account in rg-storage-prod
Add an IP rule to an account's firewall configuration
Change the access tier of a container
Enable diagnostic settings on an account
Enumerate the containers of a blob service
Upload or delete blobs through Microsoft Entra authentication

options.text: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role

explanation.correct: Storage Account Contributor permits management of storage accounts, which covers provisioning accounts and changing their configuration such as firewall rules, container access tier and diagnostic settings. The definition contains none of the container or blob data-plane permissions, so the team can't enumerate containers or upload and delete blobs with Microsoft Entra authorization, matching company policy.

perChoice.b: Reader and Data Access lets you view everything but not create or delete a storage account or a resource contained in one, so the platform team couldn't stand up accounts or reconfigure them. It also grants read/write access to all data in a storage account through account keys, which the policy forbids.
perChoice.c: Storage Blob Data Contributor grants read, write and delete on storage containers and blobs, exactly the data-plane permissions policy prohibits, and it doesn't cover managing the accounts and their configuration.
perChoice.d: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role only permits listing and regenerating storage account access keys; it can't create accounts, change firewall rules, adjust access tiers or enable diagnostics, so it doesn't satisfy the runbook.

body.stem: Your platform team is picking Azure built-in definitions for five separate duties in the prod subscription. Drag each definition to the duty that matches it.

slots.label: Must hand permissions on Azure resources to people and groups, and be able to take those permissions away again
Must create, change, and delete anything in scope, but must not be able to hand permissions to others
Must be limited to granting permissions by using Azure RBAC assignments, and must not change access by other mechanisms such as Azure Policy
Must create, change, and delete anything in scope, and must also be able to assign permissions in Azure RBAC to other identities
Must be able to view everything in scope but not change any of it

explanation.correct: Owner is the only one of the five that combines full management of every resource in scope with the ability to assign permissions in Azure RBAC to others. Contributor gives the same full management but stops short of delegation. User Access Administrator exists to manage who can reach Azure resources, without creating those resources. Role Based Access Control Administrator is the narrower delegation job and is confined to Azure RBAC, explicitly excluding other routes such as Azure Policy. Reader is view-only.

perChoice.contributor: Full management of all resources in scope, with no ability to assign Azure RBAC permissions — this is the delegation-free full-access definition.
perChoice.owner: Full management of all resources in scope plus the ability to assign Azure RBAC permissions, which is what distinguishes it from the delegation-free full-access definition.
perChoice.reader: Can view all resources but cannot make changes, so it satisfies only the view-only duty.
perChoice.rbacadmin: Manages access to Azure resources by assigning roles with Azure RBAC and explicitly cannot manage access by other routes such as Azure Policy, so it fits the RBAC-only duty.
perChoice.useraccessadmin: Lets you manage access to Azure resources for identities without creating or managing the resources themselves, which matches the duty of granting and revoking access.

body.stem: Five internal teams need narrow access to the contents of one storage account. Three work with the messaging tier and two administer the tier that is shared to Windows file servers. Drag each built-in definition to the requirement it satisfies.

items.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor

slots.label: The producer only has to place new work items into the queue so that other services can pick them up
A Windows file-server administrator may open the files and browse the folders in the shares, but must not create or change anything
A Windows file-server administrator must create, change, and delete files and folders in the shares
The consumer must look into the queue, take the next item out of it, and remove that item once it has been handled
The monitoring dashboard must list the queues and the items inside them without being able to change anything

explanation.correct: The messaging split follows what each party does with an item: adding only, taking and removing, or just listing. The two file-server duties differ only in whether changes are permitted, which is exactly the gap between the SMB share definition that allows read, write, and delete and the one that allows read only.

perChoice.filereader: Allows read access to files and directories in the file shares over SMB, so it matches the browse-only duty.
perChoice.msgprocessor: Allows a caller to look at a message, retrieve it, and delete it, which is what the consuming worker needs.
perChoice.msgsender: Only adds messages to a queue and cannot read or remove anything already there, which is what the producing service needs.
perChoice.queuereader: Reads and lists the queues and their messages but makes no changes, so it suits the monitoring dashboard.
perChoice.sharecontributor: Allows read, write, and delete on files and directories in the shares over SMB, so it fits the duty that must edit content.

body.stem: Your security team must grant four different groups the ability to sign in to servers. Drag each built-in definition to the requirement it satisfies.

rows: Servers connected to Azure through Arc
Machines hosted directly in Azure and in Azure Arc

slots.label: Must see the machine listed in the portal and sign in to it with a privileged account on the guest operating system
Must be able to grant the two sign-in privileges that exist for virtual machines to other identities, and withdraw them again
Must open an Arc-connected server in the portal and sign in with one of the accounts already set up on that server
Must see the machine in the portal and sign in to it with an ordinary account that carries no elevated rights

explanation.correct: The portal-and-sign-in definitions are separated by which kind of account is used: a privileged guest account, an ordinary guest account, or an account that was already created on an Arc-connected server. Managing that access for other people is a different job entirely and belongs to the definition that adds or removes those sign-in privileges.

perChoice.adminlogin: Lets a principal view the machine in the portal and sign in as an administrator, which matches the elevated patch requirement.
perChoice.locallogin: Is specifically for viewing the machine in the portal and signing in as an account configured on an Arc server, so it fits the field-service requirement.
perChoice.userlogin: Lets a principal view the machine in the portal and sign in as a regular, non-elevated account, matching the testing requirement.
perChoice.vmdataadmin: Manages access to virtual machines by adding or removing assignments of the two sign-in definitions, which is exactly the job of granting and withdrawing those privileges for others.

body.stem: A custom definition is being reviewed for the support team. Drag each property in the definition to what it controls.

exhibit.text:
{
  "Name": "Storage Account Monitor",
  "IsCustom": true,
  "Description": "Lets support engineers watch storage accounts and queue activity.",
  "Actions": [
    "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read",
    "Microsoft.Insights/metrics/read"
  ],
  "NotActions": [],
  "DataActions": [
    "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/queueServices/queues/messages/read"
  ],
  "NotDataActions": [],
  "AssignableScopes": [
    "/subscriptions/2f7c1d84-5b6e-4a19-9c33-7e1d0b6a4f52/resourceGroups/rg-support"
  ]
}

slots.label: Control plane operations that the definition lets a principal perform
Control plane operations taken away from what the definition would otherwise allow
Operations on the contents of the resource itself that the definition lets a principal perform
Operations on the contents of the resource itself that are taken away from what the definition would otherwise allow
The places in your tenant where the definition may be handed out
Free text that tells reviewers what the definition is meant for

explanation.correct: A definition separates management of the resource from work on its contents: one pair of properties covers the control plane and the other pair covers the data plane, and in each pair one list grants operations while the other removes operations from what would otherwise be allowed. AssignableScopes decides where the definition may be handed out, and Description is the explanatory free text.

perChoice.actions: Holds the control plane operations the definition allows, which in the review example covers reading the account and its metrics.
perChoice.assignablescopes: Lists the management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups where the definition is available for assignment, which restricts it to rg-support in the example.
perChoice.dataactions: Holds the data plane operations on the contents of the resource that the definition allows, such as reading queue messages.
perChoice.description: The explanatory free-text string shown alongside the definition.
perChoice.notactions: Holds the control plane operations excluded from the allowed list, so it subtracts from the grant rather than adding to it.
perChoice.notdataactions: Holds the data plane operations excluded from the allowed data operations, so it subtracts from the contents grant rather than adding to it.

body.stem: While troubleshooting a failed request you need to describe, in the order they happen, the checks that decide whether the caller's access is permitted. Drag each step into its stage.

items.text: Azure Resource Manager narrows the assignments down to the caller and the groups it belongs to, and works out which roles that caller holds for the resource
The caller obtains a token from Azure Resource Manager that carries its group memberships, including transitive ones, and sends its request with that token attached
If a deny assignment applies, the request is stopped right there
Azure Resource Manager gathers the role assignments and the deny assignments that apply to the resource being acted on
Any conditions carried by the assignment are evaluated, and access is allowed only while they are met
The allowed operations that contain a wildcard are reduced by the excluded operations to produce the effective management permissions

slots.label: Evaluation stage 1
Evaluation stage 2
Evaluation stage 3
Evaluation stage 4
Evaluation stage 5
Evaluation stage 6

explanation.correct: Azure Resource Manager first receives the token, then looks up the assignments and deny assignments that apply to the resource, and stops immediately if a deny assignment matches. Only after that does it narrow the assignments to the caller and its groups, work out the effective management permissions, and finally evaluate any conditions on the assignment.

perChoice.collect: Stage 2: this lookup has to happen before the deny check, because the deny check depends on what was retrieved.
perChoice.conditions: Stage 6: conditions come at the very end, once the caller is known to have the action at the requested scope.
perChoice.deny: Stage 3: a matching deny assignment blocks the request before any permission calculation continues.
perChoice.narrow: Stage 4: once nothing is denied, the assignments are filtered down to the caller and its groups.
perChoice.subtract: Stage 5: effective management permissions are computed by removing the excluded operations from the wildcard allowed ones, after the caller's roles are known.
perChoice.token: Stage 1: the caller first acquires a token that carries its group memberships and attaches it to the request.

body.stem: Your company runs all workload protection from a single backup vault, and five different people each perform one distinct job against it. Match each built-in definition to the job it belongs to.

slots.label: Create and remove the ResourceGuard tied to the vault
Carry out the critical operations that the ResourceGuard protects
Run the protection service for the vault, including deleting backup data, but no standing up new vaults or handing out access
Perform routine protection and recovery tasks, but no deleting backup data, creating vaults, or handing out access
Audit the vault's protected items and settings without changing anything

explanation.correct: The built-in roles page describes Backup MUA Admin as the definition for multiuser-authorization work that can create/delete the ResourceGuard, and Backup MUA Operator as the definition for performing the critical operation protected by that ResourceGuard. Backup Contributor manages the backup service as a whole (so it can delete backups) but cannot create vaults or give access to others. Backup Operator manages backup services except removal of backup, vault creation, and giving access to others, which covers routine protection and recovery work. Backup Reader can view backup services but cannot make changes, which is the read-only auditing duty.

perChoice.i1: Backup Contributor belongs with the duty that runs the protection service for the vault, including deleting backup data, but excludes standing up new vaults and handing out access — the documentation says it lets you manage the backup service but can't create vaults or give access to others.
perChoice.i2: Backup Operator belongs with the duty that performs routine protection and recovery tasks while excluding deletion of backup data, vault creation, and giving access to others.
perChoice.i3: Backup Reader belongs with the auditing duty, because it can view backup services but can't make changes.
perChoice.i4: Backup MUA Admin belongs with the duty of creating and removing the ResourceGuard; it is the definition for the multiuser-authorization administration work on that ResourceGuard.
perChoice.i5: Backup MUA Operator belongs with the duty of carrying out the critical operations that the ResourceGuard protects.
perChoice.i6: Disk Restore Operator fits no slot: it only provides permission to the backup vault to perform disk restore, so it is narrower than the vault-wide protection duties and isn't about audit, ResourceGuard work, or routine vault operations.

body.stem: You have field devices that post readings to an Azure Storage queue in the account stgateway01, and a separate processing service drains that queue. The gateway runs under a managed identity that must be able only to place new items in the queue; it must not be able to look at, count or remove anything already sitting in it. Which built-in role should you assign to the gateway identity at the scope of the storage account?
body.statement: The gateway's managed identity should be granted the {{role}} role at the scope of the storage account.

explanation.correct: Storage Queue Data Message Sender adds messages to an Azure Storage queue. That is exactly the single duty the gateway needs, and it leaves reading and removing queued items to the separate processing identity.

perChoice.role:a: Peek, retrieve, and delete a message from an Azure Storage queue.
perChoice.role:b: Read and list queues and queue messages.
perChoice.role:c: Read, write, and delete queues and queue messages.

body.stem: Your platform team hosts all in-network name resolution for the hub network. They must create and update the resolution resources and their record sets, but must not change the virtual networks those resources link to. Which built-in role should you assign to the team at the scope of their resource group?
body.statement: The platform team should be granted the {{role}} role at the scope of their resource group.

explanation.correct: Private DNS Zone Contributor manages the private zone resources and their record sets but grants nothing on the linked virtual networks.

perChoice.role:a: Covers public Azure DNS zones and their record sets.
perChoice.role:c: Manages networks, not the resolution resources.

body.stem: Your platform team automates permission grants. A lookup table maps each operational duty to the Azure role that should be applied, and the table is stored as readable text that operators edit by hand. Microsoft sometimes changes the wording of a role's display name, and you want the automation to keep working without anyone editing the table. Which value should the lookup table record for each duty?

columns: Role recorded in the table today

body.statement: The lookup table should record the {{identifier}} for each duty.

explanation.correct: Renaming a role never changes its ID, so automation that references the unique ID keeps working after a rename, while the built-in roles catalog lists a fixed ID for each built-in role.

perChoice.identifier:a: A rename changes this value, so assignments built from the table can start failing afterwards.
perChoice.identifier:b: Guidance text written for humans; it identifies nothing to the platform.
perChoice.identifier:c: It lists where a role may be assigned, not which role definition it is.

body.stem: Your operations team must be able to give colleagues sign-in rights to Azure virtual machines by creating and removing assignments of the two built-in sign-in roles, and your security group requires every such assignment to be constrained by conditions so that it applies only to named machines or within a time window. Which built-in role should you assign to the operations team at the scope of the subscription?
body.statement: The operations team should be granted the {{role}} role at the scope of the subscription.

explanation.correct: This role exists to hand out and take back the two sign-in roles: it adds or removes assignments for them and carries a condition that constrains those assignments.

perChoice.role:a: It lets a person sign in as administrator; it grants no right to create assignments.
perChoice.role:b: It lets a person sign in as a regular user only.
perChoice.role:c: It lets a person sign in as a local user set up on the Arc server.

body.stem: Every business application in your company runs on Azure App Service, and all of them sit in the resource group rg-apps. Two teams work there side by side. The infrastructure team owns the hosting configuration that sits underneath the applications — how many instances run, how large each instance is, and the thresholds at which the service grows or shrinks by itself — but it never publishes or edits the business applications themselves, which are the application team's responsibility. The application team publishes and maintains those applications and must leave the hosting configuration alone. Both groups hold only view access in rg-apps today. Which built-in roles should you assign at the scope of rg-apps?
body.statement: The infrastructure team should receive {{infraRole}}, and the application team should receive {{appRole}}.

explanation.correct: App Service separates the hosting construct that holds the shared infrastructure for a group of apps from the individual apps themselves, and Azure splits its built-in definitions along exactly that line. Web Plan Contributor covers the web plans for websites — the object that decides instance count, instance size, and autoscale behaviour — and it lets the infrastructure team change those settings without giving it any way to touch the business applications or to assign roles. Website Contributor is the mirror image: it covers the apps (code deployments, app settings, connection strings, and the like) while explicitly excluding the plans, so the application team gets what it needs and keeps its hands off the hosting configuration. Together the two narrow Contributor definitions give each team exactly its own slice of the resource group.

perChoice.infraRole:b: Website Contributor covers the individual applications and deliberately leaves out the plans that hold them, so the infrastructure team would still be unable to change instance counts, instance sizes, or autoscale thresholds.
perChoice.infraRole:c: Contributor grants management of everything in the resource group, including the hosting configuration and the applications owned by the other team, so it is broader than this team's remit and the least-privilege test fails.
perChoice.infraRole:d: Reader only permits viewing: the team could inspect the hosting configuration but could not change instance counts or sizes.
perChoice.appRole:a: Web Plan Contributor covers only the plans that hold the applications, so the application team would not be able to publish or maintain its own apps.
perChoice.appRole:c: Contributor grants management of everything in the resource group, which would include the hosting configuration the application team is required to leave alone.
perChoice.appRole:d: Reader is view-only, so the application team could not publish changes or update application settings.

body.stem: A media company mounts the renders container of its storage account stmedia01 as a shared Linux filesystem for a rendering farm. The team that supports the farm must be able to create and delete containers, upload and remove blobs, and also set the read, write and execute permission bits that the farm's processes run under. The current state of the account and the team's grants is shown below. Which built-in role should you assign to the team?

rows: renders container, mounted by the rendering farm over CIFS
Let the rendering service account have full control of the container's POSIX permission bits

body.statement: You should assign the {{role}} built-in role to fabrikam-renderfarm-admins at the scope of the stmedia01 storage account.

explanation.correct: The team needs full management of containers and blob content, plus the ability to control POSIX access control on containers so the rendering farm's processes get the permission bits they run under. Storage Blob Data Owner is the built-in role that combines full access to blob containers and data with assigning POSIX access control, so it satisfies both parts of the change request. Assigning it at the scope of the stmedia01 storage account keeps the grant bounded to that account.

perChoice.role:a: Storage Blob Data Reader only lists containers and reads blob content. It cannot create or delete containers, upload or remove blobs, or change container permissions, so it fails both parts of the requirement.
perChoice.role:b: This role already covers creating and deleting containers and uploading and deleting blobs, but it does not include assigning POSIX access control, so the team still could not set the container permission bits the farm relies on.
perChoice.role:d: Storage Blob Delegator only grants permission to obtain a user delegation key, which is used to mint a short-lived shared access signature for a container or blob. It gives no container or blob management rights and no control over container permissions.
